Introduction
In this study, we considered how individuals with autism (the ‘AT sample’), in
comparison with neurotypical individuals (the ‘NT sample’), engage with the built
heritage around them, how their differing perception of buildings affects the attach-
ments they formed towards them, and what features of those buildings they found
significant, developing the first large-scale survey of its kind. We undertook this study
in the context of two related fields of research. One is research into the character-
istics of Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC). The second is critical heritage studies,
with its focus on creating methods and perspectives that recognise diversity, differ-
ence and equality. We begin with a review of autism research before presenting the
methodology and results of our study. We then frame these results in the context of
some relevant heritage frameworks.
